title: Are Americans learning that test scores > grades?
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: In this weekly SCHOOLED roundup, Mike Petrilli argues that parents may finally be recognizing grade inflation, citing a Learning Heroes poll showing double-digit drops in parents who think their child is at or above grade level. He ties this to Nikole Hannah-Jones's account of discovering her daughter's A's masked weak algebra, and gathers reactions from Kelsey Piper, Roland Fryer, Jay Caspian Kang, Charles Cole III and others. He then draws on Kevin Huffman and Liz Cohen to argue that the most tractable fix is getting better data to parents, including through AI tools such as a parent-facing app being piloted in Texas. Further sections cover Matt Kraft's warning that the New York Times ranking of 30 school reforms must weigh implementation feasibility, Rick Hess's forecast of a post-midterm oversight surge, the federal scholarship tax credit regulations, a curated list of other edu-opinions, and a Manhattan Institute and Fordham exchange on school discipline compromise.
points: Learning Heroes data suggest parents are beginning to doubt that A grades signal mastery, which Petrilli treats as a possible breakthrough on grade inflation.
The most tractable lever, per Kevin Huffman, is training parents to treat a falling test score as an alarm rather than reforming grading practices across millions of teachers.
AI may help parents interpret scores and homework, and a free parent-facing advisor app is being piloted with a goal of launching first in Texas.
Matt Kraft's point that many highly ranked reforms work only if implemented well means feasible, modest-return interventions deserve more attention than they get.
On school discipline, several contributors converge on emphasizing classroom management, evidence-based behavior supports and professional development over arguments about racial disparities.
quotes: Grades can give the false impression that students are on track. A Learning Heroes survey suggests parents are beginning to question what schools tell them.

Student grades ought to reflect how well a student is doing. If a student is getting good grades, their parents ought to be able to assume that they’re adequately academically prepared for the next year’s material.
But solving this problem is hard. The first step is getting better information to parents.

The most tractable lever is shifting parent default behavior: When a MAP score drops or a child is below grade level, alarms should go off. Getting parents to treat test data as a default signal is more achievable than reforming grading across millions of teachers.
Interventions with modest ROIs but that are very feasible to implement should be seen as attractive.

The worst outcome of all is pursuing high ROI reforms while failing to consider and prepare for their implementation challenges. This leads to the all-too-familiar pattern of high hopes and dashed expectations, where reformers are quick to cut bait with little to show for their efforts.
Democratic leadership will want to focus on the things they judge most likely to resonate while avoiding narrative overload.

Rather than concentrating primarily on disciplinary disparities, I suggest instead that we emphasize high-quality classroom management, evidence-based behavior supports, and strong professional development for educators.
